kind: lemma
title: Finite-prior Bayes envelopes converge under pointwise LAN
status: draft

sources:
  references:

      url: https://sites.stat.washington.edu/jaw/COURSES/EPWG/stflour.pdf
    - title: "John Duchi, A few notes on contiguity, asymptotics, and local asymptotic normality, Theorem 3 and proof, pp. 17–18; local finite-prior proof supplied here"
      url: https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/Notes/contiguity-and-asymptotics.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume AC. In a pointwise LAN experiment [[def-lan-experiment]] with $K\succ0$, fix $h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb R^d$ and weights $w_i>0$ summing to one. Let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Lipschitz. The Bayes values for estimating $h$ with loss $g(a-h)$ and this finite prior, allowing all measurable randomized rules, converge to the corresponding Bayes value in the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$. No likelihood-field uniformity or measurable-selection hypothesis is required.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the pointwise LAN experiment, finite prior and bounded Lipschitz loss.

[F1] [[def-lan-experiment]] gives mean-one likelihood proxies $L_{n,h}$, pointwise total-variation approximation, and $\log L_{n,h}=h^T\Delta_n-h^TKh/2+o_P(1)$ with $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$.

[F2] [[thm-vector-slutsky]] and [[thm-continuous-mapping-theorem]] give joint finite-dimensional convergence after adjoining finitely many remainders that tend to zero in probability.

[F3] [[thm-mean-one-likelihood-ratio-limit-implies-contiguity]] proves uniform integrability for nonnegative mean-one variables converging in law to a mean-one limit.

[F4] [[def-bayes-and-minimax-risk]] defines the Bayes value as the infimum of prior-averaged risk over rules; [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] describes randomized rules.

[F5] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]] and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] imply $|E_Pf-E_Qf|\le M\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$ for $0\le f\le M$, by integrating the tail probabilities of $f$.

[F6] [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives a countable dense rational grid in finite-dimensional Euclidean action space by taking finite products.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is retained for the LAN and Gaussian suppliers.

## Proof

1.1 For $l\in[0,\infty)^s$, set $F(l)=\inf_a\sum_iw_i l_i g(a-h_i)$. For any $l,l'$, each action's objective changes by at most $M\sum_iw_i|l_i-l'_i|$; taking infima proves the same bound for $F$. Also $0\le F(l)\le M\sum_iw_i l_i$. For fixed $l$ the objective is continuous in $a$, so F6 makes its infimum equal to the infimum over a fixed enumeration $(q_j)$ of the rational grid. For $\epsilon>0$, choose the first $j$ whose objective is at most $F(l)+\epsilon$. This index is Borel: its defining set and the finitely many failures at smaller indices are Borel. Thus this is an explicit measurable $\epsilon$-optimal action function of $l$. [F4, F6, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Under the base law, F1 and F2 imply $(L_{n,h_i})_{i=1}^s\Rightarrow(l_i(Z))_{i=1}^s$, where $Z\sim N_d(0,K)$ and $l_i(z)=\exp(h_i^Tz-h_i^TKh_i/2)$. The log expansions imply that zero likelihoods have vanishing probability, so exponentiating the finite vector is legitimate. Gaussian integration gives $E l_i(Z)=1$. Hence $U_n=\sum_iw_i L_{n,h_i}$ converges in law to $U=\sum_iw_i l_i(Z)$ and both have mean one. F3 makes $(U_n)$ uniformly integrable. [F1, F2, F3, A1, given, construct]

2.1 For each cutoff $b$, $F\wedge b$ is bounded continuous, so its expectations converge by step 1.2. The error from this cutoff is bounded by $M E[U_n\mathbf1_{\{MU_n>b\}}]$, which vanishes uniformly as $b\to\infty$; the limit variable has the same integrable bound. Therefore $E F((L_{n,h_i})_i)\to E F((l_i(Z))_i)$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Under the proxy laws, every randomized rule has prior risk at least $E F((L_{n,h_i})_i)$ by integrating the pointwise action inequality. The explicit action rules of step 1.1 attain this lower bound within $\epsilon$, so it is exactly the proxy Bayes value after $\epsilon\downarrow0$. The same argument with $l_i(Z)$ identifies the limiting envelope expectation as the finite-prior Gaussian Bayes value: the base Gaussian $N_d(0,K)$ tilted by $l_i$ has law $N_d(Kh_i,K)$, and $Y=K^{-1}Z$ has law $N_d(h_i,K^{-1})$. Finally F5 bounds the actual/proxy risk difference uniformly over rules by $M\sum_iw_i\|P_{n,h_i}-L_{n,h_i}P_{n,0}\|_{\rm TV}\to0$. Infima preserve this bound, proving the assertion. [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

    - title: "John Duchi, A few notes on contiguity, asymptotics, and local asymptotic normality, Theorem 3 and proof, pp. 17–18; local finite-prior proof supplied here"
      url: https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/Notes/contiguity-and-asymptotics.pdf

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $Q_h=N_d(h,S)$ with $S\succ0$ and let $g:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ have Lipschitz constant $B<\infty$. For every Borel probability prior $\pi$ on $\mathbb R^d$ and $\epsilon>0$, there is a finite-support prior $\pi_f$ whose Bayes value for loss $g(a-h)$ differs from that of $\pi$ by less than $\epsilon$. The comparison is uniform over all measurable randomized rules. In particular this applies to every diffuse Gaussian prior; no posterior selector assumption is needed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the Gaussian shift, bounded Lipschitz loss, prior and accuracy.

[F1] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] gives the nondegenerate Gaussian density proportional to $\exp[-(y-h)^TS^{-1}(y-h)/2]$.

[F2] [[thm-dominated-convergence]] passes pointwise limits under an integrable envelope through an integral.

[F3] [[def-bayes-and-minimax-risk]] and [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]] define the prior risk and its infimum over randomized rules.

[F4] [[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]] and [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] give the bound $|E_Pf-E_Qf|\le M\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$ for $0\le f\le M$.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] gives compactness of closed bounded parameter balls.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is retained for the Gaussian construction.

## Proof

1.1 The map $h\mapsto Q_h$ is continuous in total variation. Indeed, when $h_j\to h$, the Gaussian densities converge pointwise. On a fixed bounded set of shifts, positive definiteness of $S^{-1}$ and $2uv\le u^2/2+2v^2$ bound all these densities by $C\exp(-c\|y\|_2^2)$ for constants $C,c>0$. This is integrable, so F2 gives $L^1$ convergence, which bounds the event-supremum total variation. On a compact ball this continuity is uniform: otherwise sequences of shifts in that ball with distances tending to zero but separated TV distances have a common convergent subsequence by F5, contradicting continuity and the TV triangle inequality. [F1, F2, F5, A1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a randomized rule $\delta_y(da)$, write $R_\delta(h)=\int\int g(a-h)\delta_y(da)Q_h(dy)$. Change the loss argument first and the sampling law second. F4 yields $|R_\delta(h)-R_\delta(h')|\le B\|h-h'\|_2+M\|Q_h-Q_{h'}\|_{\rm TV}$, independently of the rule. Each risk is between zero and $M$. Its measurability follows by integrating the jointly Borel integrand against the rule kernel and the explicit jointly measurable Gaussian density, using nonnegative simple approximations and Tonelli. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Choose a closed ball with discarded prior mass less than $\tau$. Partition that ball into finitely many Borel cells of diameter at most $\eta$ and assign one representative to each nonempty cell; send all points outside the ball to zero. This Borel finite-valued map $q$ gives $\pi_f=\pi\circ q^{-1}$. On the ball, step 1.2 bounds $|R_\delta(h)-R_\delta(q(h))|$ by $B\eta+M\omega(\eta)$, where the compact-ball TV modulus satisfies $\omega(\eta)\to0$ by step 1.1. Outside, use $M$. Consequently the prior risks differ uniformly over rules by at most $B\eta+M\omega(\eta)+M\tau$. Choose the ball first for an arbitrarily small tail and then the cell diameter small enough on that fixed ball. This makes the bound less than $\epsilon$; infima over the same rules preserve it. [F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra] ∎

    - title: "John Duchi, A few notes on contiguity, asymptotics, and local asymptotic normality, Theorem 3 and proof, pp. 17–18; local finite-prior proof supplied here"
      url: https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/Notes/contiguity-and-asymptotics.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex, with $M>0$. For integers $N\ge2$ and $m\ge1$, put $\delta=M/N$, $C_k=\overline{\{x:L(x)\le k\delta\}}$ and
$$g_{N,m}(x)=\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\min(1,m\,d(x,C_k)).$$
For $C_k=\varnothing$ the corresponding summand is defined to be one, and for $C_k=\mathbb R^d$ it is zero. Then $0\le g_{N,m}\le L$, and $g_{N,m}$ is bounded and Lipschitz. For every nondegenerate Gaussian $H\sim N_d(b,S)$,
$$\inf_a E g_{N,m}(a-H)=E g_{N,m}(H-b),\qquad
\lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{m\to\infty}E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E L(H-b).$$
Each summand is symmetric and quasi-convex; no quasi-convexity of their sum is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the bounded bowl-shaped loss, integers and Gaussian law.

[F1] [[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]]: distance to a nonempty set is one-Lipschitz.

[F2] [[lem-boundary-of-convex-set-is-lebesgue-null]]: the boundary of a convex set is Lebesgue-null, including lower-dimensional convex sets.

[F3] [[lem-gaussian-centering-for-bounded-symmetric-quasiconvex-loss]]: a bounded Borel symmetric quasi-convex loss has least Gaussian shift risk at the Gaussian center.

[F4] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]]: a nondegenerate Gaussian has a Lebesgue density.

[F5] [[thm-dominated-convergence]] passes limits of functions bounded by $M$ through the Gaussian expectation.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is retained for the Gaussian and centering suppliers.

## Proof

1.1 Each $C_k$ is closed, convex and symmetric. For a nonempty closed convex $C$, its distance is convex: choose points of $C$ within $\epsilon$ of the two infimal distances, take their convex combination, and apply the norm triangle inequality; let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Its distance is also symmetric when $C=-C$. Thus $q(x)=\min(1,m d(x,C))$ is symmetric and has convex sublevel sets: for $0\le t<1$ its sublevel is $\{d(x,C)\le t/m\}$, and for $t\ge1$ it is the whole space. It is Borel and $m$-Lipschitz by F1. The empty and whole-space conventions are constant functions with the same properties. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 If $L(x)\le k\delta$, then $x\in C_k$ and the $k$th term is zero. Every remaining term is at most one, so $0\le g_{N,m}(x)\le\delta\#\{1\le k<N:k\delta<L(x)\}\le L(x)$. The finite sum is bounded by $M$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $M m$. Apply F3 separately to each summand. Every summand's expected loss is minimized at $a=b$ (use its symmetry to replace $b-H$ by $H-b$), so the same action minimizes their sum. This proves the first displayed identity without assuming the sum quasi-convex. [F3, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Since $C_k$ is closed, its $k$th term increases to $\mathbf1_{C_k^c}$ as $m\to\infty$. The difference between $\{L>k\delta\}$ and $C_k^c$ is contained in the boundary of the convex set $\{L\le k\delta\}$, which is null by F2. By F4, it is null under the centered Gaussian as well. Therefore F5 gives $\lim_m E g_{N,m}(H-b)=E[\delta\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}\mathbf1_{\{L(H-b)>k\delta\}}]$. The expression inside the expectation differs from $L(H-b)$ by at most $\delta$: count the grid thresholds strictly below each value in $[0,M]$. Let $N\to\infty$ to obtain the second identity. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

kind: theorem
title: Local asymptotic minimax bound under compact-uniform LAN
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: mathematical-statistics-foundations-37

deps:

  - thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure

  - def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws
  - def-axiom-of-choice
  - def-euclidean-inner-product
  - def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn
proof_strategy: Bayesian lower bound and Gaussian prior limit
provenance:
  statement: literature-derived
  proof: ai-altered
sources:
  references:
    - title: John Duchi, A few notes on contiguity, asymptotics, and local asymptotic normality, §4.1, PDF pp. 17–18
      url: https://web.stanford.edu/class/stats300b/Notes/contiguity-and-asymptotics.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be a measurable local
experiment with base law $P_{n,0}$, positive-definite LAN information $K$,
central sequence $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,K)$, and supplied mean-one
likelihood proxies $L_n(h)P_{n,0}$. In addition to pointwise LAN, assume the
following **compact-uniform likelihood-field condition**: for every compact
$H\subset\mathbb R^d$,
$$\sup_{h\in H}\|P_{n,h}-L_n(h)P_{n,0}\|_{\rm TV}\to0,
\qquad E_{P_{n,0}}\sup_{h\in H}
\left|L_n(h)-e^{h^T\Delta_n-h^TKh/2}\right|\to0,$$
and the displayed suprema and posterior Bayes envelopes below are measurable.
For the Gaussian priors used in the proof, assume the posterior envelopes
admit measurable $\epsilon$-optimal action rules for every $\epsilon>0$.
This uniform condition is an additional hypothesis; it is not asserted to
follow from pointwise LAN or from the QMD-to-LAN theorem.

Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric
($L(-x)=L(x)$), and quasi-convex (each sublevel set is convex). Then
$$\liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c}
E_{P_{n,h}}L(\widehat h_n-h)
\ge E L(Z),\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K^{-1}).$$
The infimum ranges over measurable, possibly randomized, estimators. This is
the local asymptotic minimax bound with precision $K$ under the explicit
compact-uniform interface above.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the measurable local experiment and compact-uniform LAN
conditions in the statement; $K\succ0$; and the stated bounded symmetric
quasi-convex loss.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is assumed for the multivariate Gaussian
construction and its standard normal representation.

[F1] [[def-lan-experiment]]: A LAN experiment has a Gaussian central-sequence
limit and mean-one likelihood proxies with the local log-likelihood expansion.
The extra compact-uniform condition is stated separately in the theorem.

[F2] [[lem-compact-uniform-lan-posterior-approximation]]: For every compact
prior, the posterior density under the proxy experiment is close in expected
$L^1$ to the Gaussian-shift posterior; the prior-predictive central sequence
converges to its Gaussian-shift mixture.

[F3] [[lem-gaussian-centering-for-bounded-symmetric-quasiconvex-loss]]: Under
a Gaussian posterior $N(m,S)$ with $S\succ0$, the posterior expected loss
$E L(a-H)$ is minimized at $a=m$, with minimum $E L(N(0,S))$.

[F4] [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] and
[[def-bayes-and-minimax-risk]]: Risk is expectation of loss under the
parameter law; worst-case risk is at least prior-averaged risk, and the
Bayes value is the infimum of that average over decision rules.

[F5] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: Pointwise convergence under an integrable
majorant passes through the Lebesgue integral.

[F6] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]],
[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]],
[[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]], and
[[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]: A nondegenerate
multivariate normal has its usual Lebesgue density after an invertible linear
change of variables.

[F8] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: The norm $\|x\|_2$ is the Euclidean
norm used for the compact parameter balls and Gaussian densities.

[F9] [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]: Borel
measurability on $\mathbb R^d$ uses the sigma-algebra generated by its open
sets.

[F7] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]] and
[[def-total-variation-distance-for-probability-laws]]: For a bounded
nonnegative $f$, $Ef=\int_0^M P(f>t)dt$; therefore
$|E_Pf-E_Qf|\le M\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$ when $0\le f\le M$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** compactly supported Gaussian priors, posterior
approximation, then a diffuse-prior limit in the Gaussian shift.

1.1 Fix $\varepsilon>0$, put $\Gamma=\varepsilon^{-1}K^{-1}$, and for
$c>0$ let $\pi_{\Gamma,c}$ be the law $N_d(0,\Gamma)$ conditioned on
$\{\|h\|_2\le c\}$. Its support lies in the radius-$c$ ball. For every
decision rule, the supremum risk over that ball is at least its average risk
under $\pi_{\Gamma,c}$; taking the infimum over rules gives the same
inequality for the minimax and Bayes values by [F4]. [A1, F4, F8, given,
algebra]

1.2 For a loss $0\le f\le M$, [F7] implies
$|E_Pf-E_Qf|\le M\|P-Q\|_{\rm TV}$. The compact-uniform total-variation
condition therefore changes the prior-averaged risk, uniformly over all
rules, by $o(1)$ when the actual local laws are replaced by their likelihood
proxies. [F1, F7, given, algebra]

2.1 Under the proxy mixture, condition on the observation. Its posterior
$\Pi_n$ has the density in the statement of
[[lem-compact-uniform-lan-posterior-approximation]]. For any estimator, its
posterior expected loss is at least
$$r_L(\Pi_n):=\inf_{a\in\mathbb R^d}\int L(a-h)\Pi_n(dh).$$
The assumed measurability makes this a valid lower bound after integration.
Moreover, for any two posterior laws $\pi_1,\pi_2$,
$$|r_L(\pi_1)-r_L(\pi_2)|
\le M\int\left|\frac{d\pi_1}{d\pi}-\frac{d\pi_2}{d\pi}\right|d\pi$$
when they have densities relative to the same prior $\pi$; apply the bound to
each action and then take infima. [F2, F4, F9, given, algebra]

2.2 Apply [F2] with prior $\pi_{\Gamma,c}$. Step 2.1 and the expected
posterior $L^1$ approximation show that the proxy-predictive expectation of
the posterior envelope differs by $o(1)$ from the expectation of the
Gaussian-posterior envelope $R(\Delta_n)$. The function $R(z)$ is bounded
and continuous: on compact sets of $z$, the weights $e^{h^Tz-h^TKh/2}$ vary
uniformly continuously over compact $h$, so their normalized densities
converge in $L^1(\pi_{\Gamma,c})$; step 2.1 transfers this to the envelope.
The predictive weak convergence in [F2] therefore gives convergence of
$E R(\Delta_n)$ to its Gaussian-shift expectation. Every procedure's prior
average risk is at least the posterior envelope expectation; the assumed
measurable $\epsilon$-optimal rules identify the Gaussian-shift envelope
expectation with its Bayes value. Thus the proxy Bayes value has lower limit
at least the Gaussian-shift Bayes value. [F2, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.1 As $c\to\infty$, $\pi_{\Gamma,c}$ converges in total variation to the
untruncated $N_d(0,\Gamma)$ prior because its discarded Gaussian tail tends
to zero. For any event $B$, conditioning on the ball $A_c$ gives
$|\pi_{\Gamma,c}(B)-\pi_\Gamma(B)|\le\pi_\Gamma(A_c^c)$: writing
$p=\pi_\Gamma(A_c)$, $q=\pi_\Gamma(B\cap A_c)$ and
$r=\pi_\Gamma(B\cap A_c^c)$, the difference is
$|(1-p)q/p-r|$, whose two nonnegative terms are each at most $1-p$.
Thus the tail is a valid total-variation bound. For any estimator, changing the prior changes
its bounded average risk by at most $M$ times that bound; taking infima
preserves it. Since the Gaussian posterior envelopes equal the Gaussian
Bayes values by the assumed selectors, those values converge to the
full-prior Bayes value. [F4, F7, given, algebra]

3.2 In the Gaussian shift, write the observation as $Y\mid h\sim
N_d(h,K^{-1})$. Multiplying its likelihood
$\exp[-(Y-h)^TK(Y-h)/2]$ by the prior density
$\exp[-h^T\Gamma^{-1}h/2]$ and completing the square gives posterior
$$H\mid Y\sim N_d(SK Y,S),\qquad S=(K+\Gamma^{-1})^{-1}.$$
By [F3], its least posterior expected loss is $E L(N_d(0,S))$, independent
of $Y$; hence this is the full-prior Gaussian-shift Bayes value. [A1, F3,
given, algebra]

4.1 With $\Gamma=\varepsilon^{-1}K^{-1}$, one has
$S=(1+\varepsilon)^{-1}K^{-1}$. The densities of
$N_d(0,(1+\varepsilon)^{-1}K^{-1})$ converge pointwise to that of
$N_d(0,K^{-1})$ and, for $0<\varepsilon\le1$, are bounded by an integrable
constant multiple of the latter density: the former density equals
$(1+\varepsilon)^{d/2}$ times the latter density evaluated at
$(1+\varepsilon)^{1/2}x$, whose quadratic exponent is no larger. [F6]
and $0\le L\le M$ then let [F5] pass the limit through the integral and
therefore
give
$$E L(N_d(0,S))\to E L(N_d(0,K^{-1}))$$
as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. This is the required diffuse-prior limit.
[A1, F5, F6, step 3.2, given, algebra]

5.1 Steps 1.1–2.2 bound the local minimax value below by the compact-prior
Gaussian-posterior envelope; step 3.1 passes to the full Gaussian prior as
$c\to\infty$; and step 4.1 sends $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Combining these
inequalities proves the stated lower bound. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1,
step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\{P_{n,h}:h\in\mathbb R^d\}$ be a pointwise LAN experiment in the sense of [[def-lan-experiment]], with positive-definite information matrix $K$. Let $L:\mathbb R^d\to[0,M]$ be Borel measurable, symmetric and quasi-convex. Then
$$\liminf_{c\to\infty}\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c}E_{P_{n,h}}L(\widehat h_n-h)\ge E L(Z),\qquad Z\sim N_d(0,K^{-1}).$$
The infimum includes every measurable randomized estimator. Only pointwise LAN at each fixed local parameter is required: no compact-uniform likelihood approximation, joint parameter likelihood field or posterior selector assumption is imposed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the pointwise LAN experiment, $K\succ0$ and bounded Borel symmetric quasi-convex loss. If $M=0$ the conclusion is immediate, so assume $M>0$.

[F1] [[lem-finite-prior-lan-bayes-envelope-convergence]]: every fixed finite-prior Bayes value for a bounded Lipschitz loss converges to its Gaussian-shift Bayes value using only pointwise LAN.

[F2] [[lem-finite-priors-approximate-gaussian-shift-bayes-risk]]: finite priors approximate the Bayes value of any Gaussian prior in the Gaussian shift, uniformly over all randomized rules for bounded Lipschitz losses.

[F3] [[lem-bowl-shaped-loss-has-centered-lipschitz-minorants]]: bounded Lipschitz $g_{N,m}\le L$ have Gaussian posterior risk minimized at the mean, and their centered Gaussian expectations converge to those of $L$ as first $m$ and then $N$ tend to infinity.

[F4] [[def-bayes-and-minimax-risk]]: the worst-case risk over a set is at least the Bayes value for every prior supported on that set.

[F5] [[def-multivariate-normal-law]] and [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] give the usual Gaussian densities; [[thm-dominated-convergence]] permits their bounded-loss limits under an integrable envelope.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]] is retained for LAN and the Gaussian suppliers.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $N,m$ and write $g=g_{N,m}$ from F3. Set $A(c)=\liminf_n\inf_{\widehat h_n}\sup_{\|h\|_2\le c}E_{P_{n,h}}L(\widehat h_n-h)$. Since $L\ge g$, every finite prior $\pi_f$ supported in the radius-$c$ ball gives $A(c)\ge\liminf_n B_n(\pi_f,g)=B_G(\pi_f,g)$ by F4 and F1, where $B_G$ is the Gaussian-shift Bayes value. Every finite support lies in some finite ball and $A(c)$ is nondecreasing. Thus $\liminf_{c\to\infty}A(c)\ge B_G(\pi_f,g)$ for every finite prior. [F1, F3, F4, given, algebra]

1.2 Fix any positive-definite prior covariance $\Gamma$ and let $\pi_\Gamma=N_d(0,\Gamma)$. F2 supplies finite priors with Bayes values arbitrarily close to $B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)$. The left side in step 1.1 does not depend on these priors, so it is at least $B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)$. This uses only fixed finite priors when taking the LAN limit; no uniformity over a continuum of local parameters is inferred. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 In the Gaussian shift $Y\mid h\sim N_d(h,K^{-1})$, multiplying the prior and likelihood densities and completing the square gives posterior $H\mid Y\sim N_d(SK Y,S)$ with $S=(K+\Gamma^{-1})^{-1}$. By F3, every randomized action's posterior $g$-risk is at least $E g(N_d(0,S))$, and the Borel action $a(Y)=SKY$ attains it. Integrating proves $B_G(\pi_\Gamma,g)=E g(N_d(0,S))$; no measurable-selection assumption is used. [F3, F5, A1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 Choose $\Gamma=\epsilon^{-1}K^{-1}$, so $S=(1+\epsilon)^{-1}K^{-1}$. For $0<\epsilon\le1$ the density of $N_d(0,S)$ converges pointwise to that of $N_d(0,K^{-1})$ and is bounded by $2^{d/2}$ times the latter density: its quadratic exponent is more negative and its normalizing factor is $(1+\epsilon)^{d/2}$. Since $0\le g\le M$, F5 gives convergence of the expectations. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 therefore bound the stated local minimax quantity below by $E g_{N,m}(Z)$ for every $N,m$. [F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 First let $m\to\infty$ and then $N\to\infty$ in the bounds of step 2.2. F3 gives the limit $E L(Z)$, establishing the full claimed pointwise-LAN bound for all measurable randomized estimators. [F3, step 2.2, algebra] ∎
